relations.myth: Granting female creative and maternal power
relations.note: Olódùmarè grants or confirms the Mothers’ creative, maternal, and àjẹ́ power.
relations.source: Modern Òsá Méjì and related creation narratives

relations.note: Òsá Méjì carries the Mother from heaven toward earth inside his body.
The Mother refuses to leave his abdomen until goat viscera draw her out.
In alternate versions, Ọ̀rúnmìlà swallows or transports the Mothers to earth.
relations.source: Ifá scholarship and later priestly compilations

relations.note: Ọ̀rúnmìlà uses divination and sacrifice to survive and reconcile with the Mothers.
relations.source: Ifá scholarship and later priestly compilations

relations.note: Èṣù receives or conveys offerings and mediates between humans, divinities, and the Mothers.
Some priests identify Odù, womb and source of existence, with the essence of àjẹ́.
A modern interpretive complex associates female Odùduwà with primordial maternal and àjẹ́ power.
Some western-Yoruba traditions make Yemọja Gelede’s founder and senior leader of the Mothers.
Modern feminist and Afro-diasporic interpretations sometimes identify Ọ̀ṣun with the Mothers.
Egúngún masquerade may counter destructive àjẹ́, while Gelede instead placates the Mothers.
Some communities and practitioners describe Orò as a complementary male counterforce to the Mothers.
